newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African economy set for "soft landing" -Stals.
newsitem.headline: S.African economy set for "soft landing" -Stals.

text.p: South Africa's economy will slow in 1997 but should achieve a "soft landing", setting the scene for higher potential growth in 1998 and beyond, Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals told South African radio on Friday.

"The adjustments are still taking place in the economy but we are heading for what economists will refer to as a soft landing. So maybe we will be able to restore financial stability without creating too many hardships as far as real economic activity is concerned," Stals said.
Stals said the economy would not slide into recession in 1997 but growth was likely to be "slightly lower" than in 1996.

"If we maintain positive growth rates for this year, growth in 1998, 1999 and up to 2000 will be determined to an important extent by the structural adjustments that we effect in the economy now," he said.
Key elements of this programme included privatisation, further trade liberalisation and the gradual easing of exchange controls.
"If we succeed in doing these strucutural adjustments we can have good growth for the next three years."
Figures released by the Central Statistical Service on Thursday showed real South African GDP grew by a modest 3.1 percent in 1996, despite a bumper agricultural season, after 3.4 percent in 1995.
For the current year, most economists are looking for growth of two to three percent, with a decline in agriculture offsetting an expected export-led revival in manufacturing.
With the economy slowing and the rand showing relative stability so far in 1997, analysts are looking for an eventual cut in interest rates -- although perhaps not until the second half of the year.
The key Bank rate currently stands at 17 percent.
Stals told Reuters late on Thursday that a jump in money supply and private credit extension in January showed there was no scope for easing monetary policy at present.
"One should not over-react to this, and see what happens in February. But it certainly confirms that there is no room at this stage for relaxing on the monetary policy," he said.
"We've certainly not seen a very convincing decline in the rates of increase in the monetary aggregates."

South Africa's year-on-year broadly defined M3 money supply grew 16.89 percent in January, preliminary Reserve Bank figures released on Thursday showed. Annual private sector credit growth was 17.07 percent.
Both figures were considerably higher than the consensus of economists who had forecast 15.8 percent and 15.3 percent respectively.
